title: Serena Williams’s Stunning Wimbledon Return—and How to Watch It Free
summary:
The grass is pristine, the strawberries are ripe, and the tennis world is buzzing: Serena Williams is back at Wimbledon. The 23-time Grand Slam champion hasn’t competed in a major since 2022, but she’s returning as an unseeded wild card for the 139th edition of the Championships, which begin Monday, June 29 at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London.

Williams, who last won the Wimbledon singles title in 2016, is expected to play her first-round match on Monday or Tuesday. But that’s not all—she and sister Venus Williams have also received a wild card into the ladies’ doubles tournament, starting Thursday, July 2. It’s a double dose of tennis royalty, and fans won’t want to miss a single serve.

The tournament features a stacked field: Jannik Sinner, Carlos Alcaraz, Aryna Sabalenka, and Coco Gauff are all vying for the trophy. And with Wimbledon’s reputation as a celebrity magnet, you might spot Zendaya, Taylor Swift, or even Prince William and Kate Middleton in the stands.

For U.S. viewers, matches air on ESPN, ESPN2, and ABC, with first serves as early as 6 a.m. ET. No cable? No problem. Several streaming services offer free trials that include these channels. DirecTV, Hulu + Live TV, and Fubo all provide five-day free trials—enough to catch the opening rounds without paying a cent. Just remember to cancel before the trial ends if you don’t want to continue.

If you’re a die-hard tennis fan, Sling TV’s Orange & Blue plan ($60.99/month) includes ESPN and ABC, with an optional Sports Extra add-on for the Tennis Channel. ESPN Unlimited offers a standalone subscription at $29.99/month, but no free trial—though there are workarounds to watch free online.

Whether you’re rooting for Serena’s comeback or just love the elegance of grass-court tennis, this Wimbledon promises drama, nostalgia, and maybe a little royal wave. Game, set, stream!
why_it_matters: For a teenager, this story shows how sports legends can make a dramatic comeback and how access to live events is changing with streaming, teaching media literacy about free trials and subscription costs while fueling excitement for watching history unfold.

background_read: Wimbledon is the world’s oldest tennis tournament, first held in 1877 at the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club in London, and is one of the four Grand Slam events.

Serena Williams, an American tennis icon, has won 23 Grand Slam singles titles—the most in the Open Era—and has not competed in a major since the 2022 US Open, making this comeback highly anticipated.
Her sister Venus Williams, a seven-time Grand Slam champion, also received a wild card for the doubles event; the pair have won 14 Grand Slam doubles titles together.
A wild card is a special entry granted to players who might not otherwise qualify, often used to invite former champions or local favorites to boost the tournament’s appeal.

For American viewers, the ESPN network has exclusive broadcast rights, and with the rise of cord-cutting, many fans now use streaming platforms like DirecTV Stream, Hulu + Live TV, and Fubo, which offer free trials for new subscribers.

perspectives.description: Fans are thrilled to see Serena Williams return, seeing it as a chance to witness a living legend compete again and inspire a new generation of tennis players, especially young girls looking up to her.

Some skeptics argue that giving wild cards to aging stars who haven't competed recently might take opportunities away from younger, up-and-coming players grinding on the tour to earn a spot based on merit.

Media analysts point out that the proliferation of streaming options, though convenient, fragments audiences and requires consumers to navigate free trials carefully, a growing challenge in the sports broadcasting landscape.

Serena’s performance at Wimbledon could influence her legacy and decisions about retirement, while the tournament's global viewership may push streaming platforms to offer more flexible sports-only packages to meet fan demand.
